newsitem.title: FRANCE: National Front seen holding key to French election.
newsitem.headline: National Front seen holding key to French election.

text.p: Supporters of France's National Front, the far-right fringe party led by Jean-Marie Le Pen, appear to hold the key to a government victory in the parliamentary election, pollsters and analysts said on Wednesday.
"The behaviour of National Front voters in the second round appears key to the final result," Romain Pache, political director for the BVA polling firm, told Reuters.

Several recent polls have shown the current centre-right government remaining in power with a comfortable majority of National Assembly seats in the second, run-off round of the May 25-June 1 election despite winning less votes than the opposition left in the first round.

Pollsters attributed the seeming contradiction in first-round and run-off results to the expected second-round choices of National Front voters in constituencies in which the Front candidate does not survive the first round.
They said their surveys found large -- and growing -- numbers of National Front voters shifting to the centre-right candidate in the second round.
The pattern is ironic because Le Pen has been a virulent critic of conservative President Jacques Chirac in the National Assembly election campaign.
He has said his top priority is to oust Chirac's majority from power, even if it meant a victory for the left.
"Vote them out," is the party's main campaign slogan.
A Louis Harris poll for Valeurs Actuelles magazine showed the combined left with 41 percent of the first-round vote to 37.5 percent for the centre-right and 14.5 percent for the National Front.
In the second round, however, the centre-right would end up with a margin of at least 74 seats over the left, according to the Harris survey released on Wednesday and conducted on Monday and Tuesday.

Similarly, a BVA poll conducted three days earlier for the weekly Paris Match showed the combined left with 40 percent of the first-round vote to 37.5 percent for the centre-right and 14.5 percent for the National Front.
Yet on the second round, the centre-right would again win control in terms of assembly seats, BVA found.
Both polls showed the National Front winning at most two to three seats.
"The apparent paradox is that the left is progressing in the polls while the centre-right is slipping, yet the centre-right wins and the left loses," Pache said.
"The main reason for this is that second-round contests are most often duels between a Socialist and a candidate from the centre-right," he said.

Pache said the most recent BVA poll found that 57 percent of first-round National Front voters were saying they would switch to a centre-right candidate in a run-off, a rise of 16 percentage points over a week's time.
He said the trend showed that many of the Front's first-round voters were less than hard-core supporters and would not heed Le Pen's entreaties to vote out the right.
